newsitem.title: USA: IBM takes new step toward networked home PCs.
newsitem.headline: IBM takes new step toward networked home PCs.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. unveiled Thursday a new line of personal computers that breaks new ground in turning PCs into networked home appliances that fit conveniently in any room of a house.

IBM said it has redesigned its new Aptiva "S Series" so a user has easy access to key features -- the keyboard, floppy drive, compact disc player and monitor -- while the PC's main box can be stowed away under a desk, or perhaps a closet.
The PC systems take a number of their architectural cues from the tradition of slick, modular consumer electronics.
The new Aptiva machines are charcoal gray and have modular components that owe much of their inspiration to home stereo or television/videocasette player systems.

IBM said the "S Series" will come in four basic models running either Pentium 166 or 200 megahertz chips and have up to 3.2 gigabytes of storage capacity, the latest CD-ROM drives, modems and a variety of multimedia features.

The basic Aptiva models range in price from $2,499 to $3,099, excluding monitors, which run another $499 to $799, the prices of a 15-inch or 17-inch screen, respectively. The line is available immediately from retailers.
"It's as close to a grand slam as IBM has ever hit in the consumer market," said PC industry analyst Richard Zwetchkenbaum of International Data Corp., a Framingham, Mass.-based market research firm.

Emily Green, a Forrester Research analyst, said that while the machines offer several promising new features, their premium pricing -- complete systems start at around $3,000 -- are likely to keep them out of reach of first-time PC buyers.

She noted that the entry of Sony Corp. and several other Japanese consumer electronic giants into the U.S. home PC market is behind the drive by IBM and other established PC makers to make the latest home PCs more consumer-oriented.

Jose Garcia, general manager of IBM's consumer desktop unit, said, "The Aptiva split system creates a better fit between consumers and their home computers by directly addressing their distinct usage, space and styling requirements."

But while these "split system" machines mark a significant departure from the clunky, all-in-one, beige boxes that dominate corporate offices, IBM's new home PC line borrows an insight from corporate personal computer systems.

By separating the central processing unit from the essential user controls, IBM said it was paving the way for creating home computer networks similar in key respects to the local area networks that now dominate office PC systems.

The new Aptivas reflect IBM's vision of extending home computers by locating "access stations" in rooms throughout the house that serve a variety of specialised functions, in effect turning the home into a computer local area network.

These smaller computing units would be linked to a powerful server, or central processing machine, that could deliver entertainment or video games to the living room or housekeeping and business tools to the study.
A home's lighting, heating, telephone and Internet communications, security and even lawn sprinkler systems could be managed in this way, according to IBM officials.
Eventually such systems could act as a bridge from the home to cable, phone and utility companies.
Besides the stand-alone media console that houses the CD-ROM and floppy disk drives and power controls, the new Aptivas offer several other innovative features.

Its RingCentral software turns the PC into a telephone, answering machine, fax and e-mail system, allowing a user to call home and ask the PC to read back electronic mail messages, using unique IBM voice translation technology.

The software also includes a caller identification feature that allows the user to record specific messages for different callers. A call placed from the phone number of one's mother would trigger a message for her only, for example.
IBM stock was up 87.5 cents at $127.375 in early trading Thursday on the New York Stock Exchange.
